description: Harvesting the personal names that stand on a page no article claims. A contents page and a masthead are the two places a magazine prints the most names and the least prose, and they are exactly the pages the grouping walk leaves unassigned, so they carry no article brief and the names on them reach the model with the least context of anywhere in the document. The F1 and F2 reviews found them surviving in their source script there more than anywhere else. The answer is not more prompt: it is to put those names in front of a person once, and to let the ruling reach the model through the glossary channel that already exists. What is declared here is only the harvest, which is deterministic and calls no model. min_words and max_words bound how many words a candidate may hold; a single word is not evidence of a name and a long run is a sentence. max_word_chars and min_word_chars bound each word. A candidate is a run of capitalised words, optionally joined by one of name_particles, and it is rejected when any of its words is in stopwords -- the closed class words and month names a capitalised run picks up at the start of a sentence -- or when any of its words is in institution_words, which are the words a name of an organisation, a publication or a place is built from rather than a person. all_caps_max_words bounds how many words of a candidate may be written in capitals throughout: a masthead sets a person's name in capitals and also sets its own wordmark there, and a long all capitals run is a wordmark. A candidate already carried by a glossary the run holds is dropped, because it is already decided. The three lists are matched without regard to case, because a masthead sets a role in capitals and a role is not a name at either case. Nothing here names a publication, a person or a place: every list is of word forms, and a list that named one would be a rule about one magazine rather than about magazines. render_batch_max bounds how many names one rendering request may ask about. The answer is one array with an entry per name, so a long enough list runs the reply into the engine's output ceiling and comes back truncated rather than refused -- and a truncated JSON array parses as nothing at all, which on this corpus silently left eighty names defaulting to themselves. The bound is on the request rather than on the harvest, so nothing is dropped: a table longer than the bound is asked about in several requests.
